title: Demonstrative and Relative Pronouns

objectives.text: recognize the various forms of the demonstrative pronouns ἐκεῖνος (that) and οὗτος (this),
objectives._source: Objectives page WordSelection table, 11_DEMON.TBK 0x5e176 region (VERIFY-5H (o): both speak in the original).

objectives: translate demonstrative pronouns and identify how they function within the syntax of the sentence,
recognize the various forms of the relative pronoun,

content.text: We will explore three types of pronouns in this chapter. Pronouns are words used in place of one or more nouns. We have already looked at personal pronouns (he, she, it, I, you, they).
In this chapter we will examine four new types of pronouns: demonstrative, relative, reflexive and reciprocal.
[[u]]Demonstratives[[/u]] are pointers. They point to things near ("this/these") or things far ("that/those"). "These" and "those" are the plural forms.
Demonstratives may function like [[u]]adjectives[[/u]] when they modify a word, or like [[u]]pronouns[[/u]] when they stand alone.

Adjective: "He bought [[u]]this[[/u]] computer."
Pronoun: "[[u]]This[[/u]] is the computer."
Relative pronouns are words like: who, whom, which, that and whose.
They are often embedded in clauses that modify a noun. "Who" is usually used for humans and "which" for non-humans. "Whose" is used for both.

The student [[u]]who[[/u]] loves Greek will succeed.
The keys [[u]]which[[/u]] were lost in the river are gone forever.

[[u]]Reflexive[[/u]] pronouns are used to indicate that the antecedent is acting on itself. This is similar to one of the functions of the middle voice in Greek.
Terry threw [[u]]himself[[/u]] into the water from the bridge.

[[u]]Reciprocal[[/u]] pronouns are used to indicate that several subjects are acting on each other.
They loved [[u]]one another[[/u]].

content.text: These can function either like a pronoun (when they stand alone) or like an adjective (thus agreeing with their antecedent in gender, number and case).

content.label: Demonstratives

content.text: When they are adjectival, the noun has the definite article and the demonstrative does not. It is then translated as an attributive adjective (e.g. "this book").
Note that this is the opposite of other adjectives which when found without the article are translated as predicate adjectives (e.g. "The book is red").

topics.title: Introduction

content.text: A relative pronoun often introduces a subordinate clause relating one word or idea to this clause. They agree with their antecedent in gender and number. Their case is determined by their role in the sentence or clause. Relatives are usually translated as "who" or "whom" for humans and "which" for neuter. "That" and "whose" can be used for either humans or non-humans. (Mounce, p. 109)

items: Sometimes the relative pronoun will have the case of its antecedent rather than the case that it should have within its own clause.
Sometimes the antecedent is understood in the context and not explicitly stated.

topics.title: Reflexive/Reciprocal

content.text: Reflexive pronouns specify an action the subject makes on itself. Because αὐτός is used in the nominative in this regard the reflexive pronouns are found only in the genitive, dative and accusative cases. These are translated "myself, yourself..."
ἀλλήλων ("one another") is the reciprocal pronoun. It specifies interaction of members within a group.
